lines.trans: See you!

meanings.note: Agrees with the speaker's gender: a man says أنا آسف, a woman says أنا آسفة.

examples.trans: I am very sorry for the delay.
Sorry for the bother, sir.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for both casual 'yes / yeah' and 'oh! / ah!' upon noticing something.

examples.trans: Oh, the door opened! Thank you.
Yes, eight rooms and eight keys.

meanings.note: Everyday adverb 'sometimes'.

examples.trans: Sometimes air gets into the pipes at night.
Sometimes we have tea in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أسابيع.

examples.trans: Next week I have time off.
We stayed at the guesthouse all week.

meanings.note: Polite Jordanian title for any man ('sir / Mr') as well as 'teacher' or 'professor'.

examples.trans: Please have a seat, sir.
Good morning, gentlemen.

meanings.note: Subject pronoun 'I' for any speaker.

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I am Salma from the kitchen.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بنقذ, بينقذ).

examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast!
You saved my whole trip.

meanings.note: Exclamation of mild surprise or realization ('oh!').

examples.trans: Oh! My glasses are on my head!
Oh, look at the beauty of this ceiling!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: I am very sorry for the disturbance.
There is no bother at all.

meanings.note: Introduces 'that'-clauses with pronoun suffixes (إنه 'that', إني 'that I', إنك 'that you', إنها 'that she/it') and appears in إن شاء الله ('if God wills').

examples.trans: Thank you for coming today.
Do you think that I am a hotel inspector?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: The reception desk is beside the door.
Thank you for the warm welcome.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (ببرد, بيبرد).

examples.trans: The cake is cooling on the rack right now.
The radiator is starting to get cold at the bottom.

meanings.note: Extremely common Jordanian word meaning both 'only / just' (بس نص كاسة 'just half a glass') and 'but' between clauses.

examples.text: بدي أقرأ الدفتر، بس مش ملاقي نظارتي!
examples.trans: I want to read the ledger, only I cannot find my glasses!
Just half a glass, please.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('under, beneath') and standalone ('downstairs').

examples.trans: Let us bring it downstairs into the light.
The wide desk is under the window.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun.

examples.trans: The heating is working in all the rooms.
The heating pipe is warm now.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: جلود.

examples.trans: This is a small brown leather notebook.
The leather bag is heavy and sturdy.

meanings.note: Everyday word for 'next to, beside'.

examples.trans: Put a napkin beside every cup.
There is no light beside the bed.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('inside the bag') and standalone ('inside').

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
The water is flowing inside!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: The iron gate is locked at night.
Pass me the heavy iron wrench.

meanings.note: In Jordanian household speech, حرام (plural حرامات) is the everyday word for a warm bed blanket.

examples.trans: I have a warm wool blanket on the bed.
We brought clean blankets from the closet.

meanings.note: Core word in صباح الخير ('good morning'), مساء الخير ('good evening'), تصبح على خير ('good night'), and rising-tone خير؟ ('is everything okay?').

examples.trans: Good morning, neighbours!

examples.text: خير إن شاء الله، شو صار؟
examples.trans: Hopefully all is well, what happened?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: دافية, plural: دافيين).

examples.trans: The bread is warm and fresh from the oven.
Sitting in the attic is cozy when it rains.

دخل.gloss: to enter; come in; go in

meanings.en: to enter; come in; go in
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بدخل, بيدخل).

examples.text: تفضل ادخل من المطر يا أستاذ.
examples.trans: Please come in out of the rain, sir.

examples.text: الزوجين دخلوا غرفة ستة قبل ساعة.
examples.trans: The couple checked into room six an hour ago.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: دفايات.

examples.trans: The radiator in the corner started warming up.
We turned on the heaters when it got cold.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: دفاتر.

examples.trans: We wrote the name in the booking ledger.
I forgot my leather notebook on the table.

meanings.note: Covers daqqa ('a knock / clock chime', pl. دقات) and diqqa ('precision / punctuality', الدقة بالمواعيد).

examples.text: سمعنا اطنعشر دقة من برج الساعة.
examples.trans: We heard twelve chimes from the clock tower.
I always love punctuality.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بدور, بيدور).

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.
Look for a blue wooden door.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Levantine future marker placed before a subjunctive verb (without ب-).

examples.text: ضيفة غرفة أربعة رح تقعد كل الأسبوع.
examples.trans: Room four's guest will stay all week.

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day is not going to be boring!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: زوايا.

examples.trans: The corner shop opens early.
I love the corner pieces of lemon cake.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ساحات.

examples.trans: The courtyard has a big jasmine tree.
We sat drinking tea in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسمع, بيسمع).

examples.trans: Did you hear the gate bell downstairs?
Inside the courtyard we hear the tree leaves.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شوارع.

examples.trans: Our guesthouse is on a quiet street in central Amman.
There are old stone streets in the quarter.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أشغال.

examples.text: حبيت الشغل هون من أول يوم.
examples.trans: I loved the work here from day one.
Let us finish our work before noon.

meanings.note: Standard everyday 'thank you' across the Arabic-speaking world.

examples.trans: Thank you all very much!
Thank you for your patience, sir.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: شوربات.

examples.trans: Here is a cup of hot vegetable soup.
Hot soup is wonderful on a rainy day.

شوي.gloss: a little; a moment (شوي شوي slowly)

meanings.en: a little; a moment (شوي شوي slowly)
meanings.note: Means 'a bit / a moment' (استنوا شوي 'wait a moment'); doubled شوي شوي means 'slowly, gently'.

examples.trans: Wait a moment, I have an idea!
Turn the valve slowly and gently.

meanings.note: Construct form of شوي used directly before a noun: شوية زبدة ('a little butter'), شوية هوا ('a bit of air').

examples.text: بس شوية زبدة مع الخبز، شكرا.
examples.trans: Just a little butter with the bread, thank you.
A little air gets into it at night.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Thank you very much for your patience with us.
Patience is the key to relief.

صبّح.gloss: to wake in the morning (تصبح على خير good night)

meanings.en: to wake in the morning (تصبح على خير good night)
meanings.note: Subjunctive تصبح على خير (to a man) / تصبحي على خير (to a woman) is the standard Jordanian 'good night' ('may you wake to goodness').

examples.trans: Good night, sir!
Good night, see you at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أصواف.

examples.trans: This wool sweater is warm and soft.
A wool blanket is cosy in winter.

طلع.gloss: to go up; go out; come out; turn out

meanings.en: to go up; go out; come out; turn out
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بطلع, بيطلع).

examples.text: لفائف القرفة هلا طلعت من الفرن!
examples.trans: The cinnamon rolls just came out of the oven!
Go up the stairs to the third floor.

meanings.note: Used both to get someone's attention politely ('excuse me') and to reply to شكرا ('you're welcome').

examples.trans: Excuse me, is the door locked?
Excuse me, Mr. Rami, sorry for the bother.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'on, at, to'; before ال- it regularly contracts to عال- ('al- / 'a-).

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: Marks location ('at, by') and with pronoun suffixes expresses possession: عندي ('I have'), عندك ('you have'), عندنا ('we have').

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door.
I have a reservation under the name Suad.

meanings.note: As an adjective غريب / غريبة means 'strange, odd'; as a noun (plural غرباء) it means 'stranger(s)'.

examples.trans: I heard a strange metallic knock at night.
Why would he leave his bag with strangers?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بفحص, بيفحص).

examples.trans: Tariq will inspect the cellar right away.
We checked the heater and pipes this morning.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Breakfast is from seven thirty to ten.
We prepared a warm breakfast for the guests.

meanings.note: Adverb 'right away, at once'.

examples.trans: Count on me, I am heading out right away!
The hot water came back immediately.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('above, over') and standalone ('upstairs').

examples.trans: The window is above the old tree.
Let us go upstairs to see the room.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أقبية.

examples.trans: The boiler is down in the basement.
He went down to the cellar to get the toolbox.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: قديمة, plural: قدام).

examples.trans: The courtyard has an old jasmine tree.
The old hardware shop is past the bridge.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun suffixes: كأنها ('as if it'), كأنهم ('as if they').

examples.text: بتحكي مع الجيران كأنهم صحاب زمان.
examples.trans: She talks with the neighbours as if they were old friends.
It sounded as if it came from the heating pipe.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: كاسات.

examples.trans: Please have a glass of hot mint tea.
He poured half a glass of orange juice.

meanings.note: Arabic uses no 'is/are' in the simple present, while كان supplies the past ('was/were') and يكون / بيكون supplies future or modal 'be'.

examples.trans: How was the bus ride?

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day will not be boring!

meanings.note: Placed AFTER the adjective or verb it intensifies: تقيلة كتير ('very heavy'), شكرا كتير ('thank you very much').

examples.trans: The smell is so good!
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun كل means 'every' (كل يوم 'every day'); before a definite noun it means 'all / the whole' (كل الأسبوع 'all week').

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everyone is happy in the courtyard today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بلمس, بيلمس).

examples.trans: Touch the radiator — it is warm on top.
Touch the brass pipe — it heated up!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ليالي.

examples.trans: The guest arrived last night.
The neighbourhood is very quiet at night.

meanings.note: Definite الليلة means 'tonight', while indefinite ليلة means 'one night / night of'.

examples.trans: I am going to sleep well tonight.
We booked the room for three nights.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: مواسير.

examples.trans: The copper pipe started warming up right away.
Old pipes need maintenance in winter.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مبسوطة, plural: مبسوطين).

examples.trans: We are very glad that you liked the courtyard.
The guests left happy from breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مرتاحة, plural: مرتاحين).

examples.text: عندي حرام صوف دافي فأنا مرتاح.
examples.trans: I have a warm wool blanket, so I am comfortable.
We were glad to see you at ease.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مكاتب.

examples.trans: The keys are on the reception desk.
The wooden desk under the window is wide.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ملاحظات.

examples.trans: He wrote all the street notes in the notebook.
Thank you for that helpful observation.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition meaning 'from', 'of', or 'than' after comparatives.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مناسبة, plural: مناسبين).

examples.trans: The sweater's size fits you perfectly.
The courtyard is quiet and suitable for work.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بنسى, بينسى).

examples.trans: You forgot the notebook beside the soup bowl.
With all the rush, I completely forgot!

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian demonstrative ('this / that'); feminine هادي (haadi), plural هدول (hadool). Before ال- it also contracts to هال-.

examples.trans: Here we use this big ledger.
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: Masculine هادي ('quiet') is homographic with the feminine demonstrative هادي ('this'); context and agreement distinguish them cleanly.

examples.trans: The spot above the tree is very quiet.
We prepared the quiet attic room for you.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word for 'now / right now' (pronounced halla' in Amman).

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door now.
We will check the tag right now.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: A little air got into the old pipes.
Morning air in Amman is crisp and clean.

meanings.note: Placed directly before a name or title when addressing someone in Arabic (يا نور 'Nour!', يا أستاذ 'sir!') and in exclamations (يا سلام! 'wonderful!').

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Appears in صباح النور ('morning of light', the standard reply to صباح الخير) and نور الشمس ('sunlight').

examples.trans: Good morning and welcome!
We read the card in the sunlight.

meanings.note: Means 'before' (قبل الفطور) and with a time span 'ago' (قبل ساعة 'an hour ago', قبل شوي 'just now').

examples.text: علمت بيانو هون قبل خمسة وعشرين سنة.
examples.trans: I taught piano here twenty-five years ago.
Drink your coffee before the rush.
